newsitem.title: MEXICO: Innova notes seen hit by limited television market.
newsitem.headline: Innova notes seen hit by limited television market.

text.p: Innova, S de R.L. is set to launch a 10-year, $375 million senior note issue, but rating agencies say the start-up company faces a number of challenges in its battle to sell direct-to-home television services in Mexico.
A limited market for the digitally delivered television, among other factors, means the note issue will only receive a speculative grade rating, analysts said.
The notes could be launched as early as next week, led by Morgan Stanley.
"It is in process," said a company official who declined to be identified.
Innova is a joint venture, 60 percent owned by Grupo Televisa, 30 percent by News Corp, and 10 percent by Tele-Communications International Inc.
Rating agencies have several concerns about the market that Innova's product will have to win over, saying the targeted upper-end of the market has a limited number of subscribers.
They also say Innova will be exposed to heavy U.S. dollar costs.

"It is a start-up company and has only been offering services for about two months or so," said Moody's senior analyst Robert Konefal. "They are not profitable yet and probably won't be for several years."
Moody's has assigned a B2 rating to the notes issue, which is a speculative grade.
Standard & Poor's, as well, has assigned a single B-minus rating to the proposed issue, with a stable outlook.
"It is not an investment-grade rating - it is a speculative rating," said S&P analyst Andrea Esposito.
She noted that a limited number of upper- and middle-income subscribers may not be able to support two satellite television services.
S&P said its rating also reflects Innova's limited capital base relative to potential cash needs.
Innova launched its service late last year, offering 60 channels on digital video.
The company is going head-to-head with joint venture DirecTV, which offers a similar service but has a head start. Innova also faces competition from cable television in Mexico City, analysts say.

"The (Moody's) rating reflects the start-up nature of the venture: the need for substantial investments for subscriber equipment, marketing, transponder leases, and other operating costs; and the uncertainty of subscription levels for the service, which is targeted, due to its cost, only to the top 25 percent of the population in terms of household income," Moody's said.
Both rating companies point to the fact that Innova's revenues will be in pesos, while operating costs, including interest, will be for the most part in dollars.
On the positive side, Innova will have access to the deep library resources of both Televisa and News Corp.
The two television giants will be able to assist Innova in its launch and with infusing equity capital.
The senior notes are being sold in privately negotiated transactions, and the first three years of interest will be paid out of a restricted escrow account, Moody's said.
